analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from forcing customers into private arbitration over safety hazards.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from March 2017 until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies often write contracts — for credit cards, phones, nursing homes, jobs — that force customers and workers to settle disputes in private arbitration instead of court. This bill said that when a claim involves a danger to public health or safety, arbitration could only be used if the customer agrees to it after the dispute happens, not because of fine print signed years earlier. It also required arbitrators to explain their decisions in writing, publicly. The bill was introduced by Senator Whitehouse and seven Democratic colleagues, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and workers with forced-arbitration clauses in their contracts. When someone is harmed by an unsafe product, a nursing home, a loan, or working conditions, they could take the company to public court instead of a private arbitrator, and their case would create a public record rather than a sealed one.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and workers in arbitration contracts

how_it_helps.text: The bill blocks pre-dispute arbitration clauses from being used to force a person out of court when the claim involves facts relevant to a hazard to public health or safety; arbitration could proceed only with written consent from all parties after the dispute arises [S2][S3].

It requires any arbitrator who hears such a case to give a written explanation of the factual and legal basis for the outcome, and that explanation cannot be kept under seal — meaning safety-related disputes become public rather than hidden [S2][S3].
The changes apply only to contracts signed after enactment, so people would know before they sign whether the protection applies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that put forced-arbitration clauses in consumer and employment contracts — banks, lenders, phone and cable companies, nursing homes, manufacturers, and large employers — would face more lawsuits in open court and greater exposure to public scrutiny and class actions.

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue arbitration is faster and cheaper for consumers than court litigation, and that banning it in safety-related cases could increase litigation costs that get passed into prices [S2].

The bill's definition of a 'hazard to public health or safety' — any activity, substance, or condition with the potential to harm the public — is very broad [S3], so it could sweep in many ordinary contract disputes that companies say belong in arbitration, creating uncertainty over which forum applies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: forced arbitration has been shown to make it harder for people to band together and to keep outcomes private, while arbitration can be quicker and cheaper in individual cases. This bill takes the side of court access and public records for safety-related disputes, and its cost falls on companies in the form of more litigation and publicity. A fair objection is that the definition of a safety hazard is drawn so broadly that the line between covered and uncovered disputes would be contested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Whitehouse introduced the bill on March 7, 2017, joined by seven Democratic cosponsors: Senators Leahy, Murray, Durbin, Franken, Hirono, Markey, and Merkley [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S5].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the record for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies with forced-arbitration clauses are better off, because their arbitration requirements stayed fully enforceable and the public never saw a floor debate or vote on limiting them.

industries.industry: Companies using forced-arbitration clauses (banks, telecoms, nursing homes, manufacturers, large employers)
industries.note: The bill would have voided their pre-dispute arbitration clauses for safety-related claims, exposing them to public lawsuits and class actions. Their gain from the bill dying is consumers' loss of court access.
Fewer compelled safety-related arbitrations means less arbitration business, and the public-explanation requirement removes the secrecy many arbitration customers value.
